title: MS SHARMA ENTERPRISES VS. NATIONAL BUILDING CONSTRUCTION CORPORATION

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1135
1
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13782 OF 2026
(Arising out of Special Leave Petition (C) No. 17072 of 2026)
MS SHARMA ENTERPRISES ... Appellant
VERSUS
NATIONAL BUILDING
CONSTRUCTION CORPORATION ... Respondent
J U D G M E N T
VIPUL M. PANCHOLI, J.
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal challenges the final judgment and order
dated 20.03.2026 passed by the Division Bench of the High
Court of Delhi in FAO(OS) (COMM) No. 18 of 2026. By the
impugned judgment, the Division Bench dismissed the
appeal preferred by the appellant under Section 37 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (hereinafter referred to
as "the 1996 Act"), upholding the judgment of the learned

2
Single Judge dated 19.11.2025 in O.M.P. (COMM) No. 215 of
2022. The learned Single Judge had partly allowed the
petition filed by the respondent under Section 34 of the 1996
Act by setting aside the arbitral award dated 28.07.2016 to
the extent it awarded pre-reference and pendente lite interest
in favour of the appellant.
3. The dispute between the parties has a long history spanning
over three decades. As per the pleadings of the parties, the
factual matrix of the present case is as under:
3.1. The respondent, National Building Construction
Corporation Limited (hereinafter referred to as "NBCC") was
awarded works by the Indian Railway Construction Company
Limited (hereinafter referred to as "IRCON"). On 11.01.1991,
the respondent awarded a sub-contract to the appellant, M/s
Sharma Enterprises, for executing flooring and cladding
works at Vashi Railway Station-cum-Commercial Complex,
New Bombay (now Navi Mumbai), for an agreed contractual
sum of Rs.9,50,73,603.20. The works were to be completed
within a period of two years, with the stipulated completion
date being 10.01.1993.

3
3.2. The execution of the sub-contracted flooring and
cladding works was intrinsically dependent upon the
completion of civil works by M/s Mohinder Singh & Co.,
which is the civil contractor engaged by the respondent. On
account of delays and non-completion of civil works, the
appellant could execute only limited areas. The appellant
completed the priority platform areas in time for inauguration
on 09.05.1992. However, on 22.09.1992, the respondent
issued notices and formally terminated the contract,
subsequently encashing the bank guarantees of the
appellant.
3.3. The appellant invoked the arbitration clause being
Clause 10 of Special Conditions of the Contract (hereinafter
referred to as "the SCC") and sought the appointment of an
arbitrator, however, the respondent did not appoint an
arbitrator. Thereafter, the appellant approached the High
Court under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 1940
(hereinafter referred to as "the 1940 Act") for appointment of
an arbitrator. Following several rounds of litigation, this
Court, by order dated 03.08.2011 in Civil Appeal No. 6341 of

4
2011, appointed the learned Arbitrator to adjudicate all
claims and counter-claims of the parties.
3.4. On 28.07.2016, the learned Arbitrator rendered an
award holding that the respondent had wrongfully
terminated the contract and had failed to provide the
requisite work fronts. Consequently, the learned Arbitrator:
● Allowed Claim No. 1(a) for executed work to the extent
of Rs.45,653.15,
● Allowed Claim No. 1(b) towards extra items (differing
varieties/shades of granite and specialised cladding) to
the tune of Rs.26,03,465/-,
● Allowed Claim No. 2 towards bank guarantee extension
charges to the extent of Rs.2,77,500/-,
● Allowed Claim No. 3 directing refund of the encashed
bank guarantee towards security deposit amounting to
Rs.19,01,480/-,
● Awarded costs of litigation quantified at Rs.5,00,000/-
under Claim No. 6,
● Rejected all counter-claims preferred by the respondent,
and

5
● Awarded interest under Claim No. 7 at the rate of 10%
per annum on the awarded sums (except costs) with
effect from 22.09.1992 until actual payment, i.e., pre-reference, pendente lite and post-award periods.
3.5. In M/s Sharma Enterprises v. N.B.C.C. (India) Ltd. (Civil
Appeal Nos. 7701-7702 of 2021, decided on 15.12.2021), this
Court resolved the issue of the applicable statutory
framework to the proceedings and held that the arbitration
proceedings were governed by the 1996 Act and not the 1940
Act.
3.6. Thereafter, the respondent challenged the arbitral award
dated 28.07.2016 under Section 34 of the 1996 Act before the
High Court in O.M.P. (COMM) No. 215 of 2022. By judgment
dated 19.11.2025, the learned Single Judge upheld the
arbitral award on all substantive claims, holding that the
findings of the learned Arbitrator were findings of fact based
on appraisal of evidence, requiring no interference under
Section 34 of the 1996 Act. However, the learned Single Judge
set aside the award of pre-reference and pendente lite interest
on the ground that Clause 26 of the SCC operated as an
absolute bar against the grant of interest, relying upon the

6
decision of this Court in Sayeed Ahmed and Company v.
State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.1
3.7. The appellant challenged the judgment dated
19.11.2025 passed by the learned Single Judge under
Section 37 of the 1996 Act before the Division Bench of the
High Court in FAO(OS) (COMM) No. 18 of 2026. Vide the
impugned judgment dated 20.03.2026, the Division Bench
dismissed the appeal and held that the inclusion of the
phrase "or otherwise" in Clause 26 of the SCC was analogous
to the phrase "or any other respect whatsoever" interpreted in
Sayeed Ahmed (supra), thereby constituting a
comprehensive bar on pendente lite interest.
3.8. Aggrieved thereby, the appellant has filed the present
appeal.
4. Mr. Siddhartha Dave, learned senior counsel appearing on
behalf of the appellant, submitted that the present appeal
challenges the impugned judgment, affirming the judgment
of the learned Single Judge, in so far as it sets aside the
arbitral award with respect to payments of interest under
1
(2009) 12 SCC 26.

7
Claim No. 7 of the arbitral award by holding that Clause 26
of the SCC barred payment of interest. Learned counsel made
the following submissions:
4.1. It is submitted that the arbitral tribunal held that the
termination of contract by the respondent was illegal and
arbitrary, directed the return of the bank guarantee amounts
and further awarded claim towards cost of extra items
executed by the appellant. It is stated that there was no
specific bar to award pendente lite interest on the said claims.
It is further contended that the respondent did not rely upon
Clause 26 of the SCC before the Arbitral Tribunal to dispute
the award of interest.
4.2. It is submitted that Clause 26 of the SCC can neither be
read in isolation nor can be given an artificially expansive
meaning. It is stated that the settled principles of ejusdem
generis and noscitur a sociis are applicable in the present
case. The concluding words of Clause 26 of the SCC "or
otherwise" follow and qualify the preceding expressions
relating to the holding up of balance payments or deposits
and delay in making monthly or final payments. It is
contended that "or otherwise" cannot be construed as an

8
absolute prohibition against pendente lite interest, as such
an interpretation would convert a clause dealing with delayed
contractual payments into a blanket prohibition against
pendente lite interest on every claim arising under the
contract.
4.3. It is further submitted that the courts below wrongly
interpreted Clause 26 of the SCC as prohibiting interest,
because had the parties intended to impose such an absolute
prohibition, the parties would have employed clear and
unequivocal language to that effect.
4.4. Reliance is placed upon Oil and Natural Gas
Corporation Ltd. v. G&T Beckfield Drilling Services Pvt.
Ltd.2 and Ferro Concrete Construction (India) Pvt. Ltd. v.
State of Rajasthan,
3 to urge that there is a distinction
between a clause barring interest on delayed payments and
a clause expressly prohibiting pendente lite interest.
4.5. It is submitted that the High Court wrongly equated
Clause 26 of the SCC with the provisions in Sayeed Ahmed
2 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1888.
3 2025 SCC OnLine SC 708.

9
(supra) and Jaiprakash Associates Limited (JAL) through
its Director v. Tehri Hydro Development Corporation
(India) Limited (THDC) through its Director,
4 wherein the
clause expressly prohibited interest and extended "in any
other respect whatsoever".
4.6. Further reliance is placed upon the decision of this Court
in Union of India v. Larsen & Toubro Limited,
5 wherein
interest was explicitly barred on all sums and for pre-award
periods, however Clause 26 of the SCC does not provide such
a restriction.
4.7. It is further submitted that pendente lite interest is
awarded in exercise of statutory power under Section 31(7)(a)
of the 1996 Act and such power can be excluded only by clear
and express contractual language, whereas Clause 26 of the
SCC neither expressly bars interest in arbitration
proceedings nor excludes the jurisdiction of the Arbitral
Tribunal to award pendente lite interest.
4
(2019) 17 SCC 786.
5 2026 INSC 203.

10
4.8. Learned counsel for the appellant lastly submitted that
the disputes relate to the year 1992 and the parties have gone
through several rounds of litigation, therefore the learned
arbitrator rightly awarded interest in favour of the appellant
and thus, the impugned judgment is to be set aside.
5. Ms. Shilpi Chowdhary, learned counsel appearing on behalf
of the respondent, opposed the present appeal and made the
following submissions:
5.1. Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act provides for pre-award
interest subject to "unless otherwise agreed by the parties"
and thus, where parties agree to exclude interest, the
contract stipulation binds the Arbitral Tribunal and pre-reference and pendente lite interest cannot be awarded
contrary to the agreement. Reliance is placed upon Oil and
Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (supra).
5.2. It is further submitted that Clause 26 of the SCC is not
confined to delayed monthly or final payments. The
expression "or otherwise" is residuary in nature and covers
situations not specifically contemplated in the preceding
expressions and it cannot be confined to the immediately

11
preceding contingency, as that would add a restriction to
which the parties never agreed.
5.3. Reliance is placed upon the decision of Union of India
v. Manraj Enterprises,
6 wherein this Court held that where
expressions are separated by 'or' and are independent, the
latter expression cannot be restricted by applying ejusdem
generis. Further reliance is placed upon the three-judge
bench decision in Jaiprakash Associates Limited (supra),
wherein this Court held that ejusdem generis can apply only
where the preceding expressions constitute a distinct genus
or category. It is submitted that in Clause 26 of the SCC, the
expressions preceding "or otherwise" do not constitute such
a distinct genus, and thus, the principles of ejusdem generis
and noscitur a sociis are not applicable in the present case.
5.4. Further reliance is placed upon the decision in the case
of Larsen & Toubro Limited (supra), wherein this Court
reaffirmed the principles in Manraj Enterprises (supra) and
Union of India v. Bright Power Projects (India) Private
6
(2022) 2 SCC 331.

12
Limited,
7 and held that Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act gives
paramount importance to the contract and restricts the
power of an arbitrator to award pre-award or pendente lite
interest contrary to the agreement.
5.5. It is further urged that while the clause in Oil and
Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (supra) merely addressed
"delayed payment or disputed claim", the clauses in Sayeed
Ahmed (supra) and Jaiprakash Associates Limited
(supra) contained a wider prohibition. However, Clause 26 of
the SCC is materially wider and by expressly concluding with
the words "or otherwise" operates as an all-inclusive bar on
interest.
5.6. It is submitted that the reliance placed by the appellant
upon Ferro Concrete Construction (supra) is misplaced as
it is based on the 1940 Act and there was no residual clause
unlike the present case.
5.7. Learned counsel for the respondent lastly submitted that
neither equity can enlarge a contractual entitlement, nor
prolonged litigation can convert an expressly excluded right
7
(2015) 9 SCC 695.

13
into an enforceable one and therefore, the present appeal is
to be dismissed.
6. We have heard learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
parties and perused the record. The question that falls for our
determination is whether Clause 26 of the SCC operates as a
contractual bar within the meaning of Section 31(7)(a) of the
1996 Act barring the Arbitral Tribunal from awarding pre-reference and pendente lite interest on the substantive claims
allowed in favour of the appellant.
7. For convenience, it is apposite to examine Clause 26 of the
SCC, which reads as follows:
"26. The sub-contractor shall be paid monthly running bill for the quantity
already executed upto the end of previous month subject to the approval of
quantity measured unless otherwise specified. The amount so payable in the
estimated value of works shall be paid upto date, less the amount already paid.
If the monthly interim payment which become payable is not paid due to any
reason, then 75% of the works executed and measured shall be paid to the sub-contractor as advance on written request. The payment to the sub-contractor will
be released within seven days of NBCC receiving its payment from the clients
i.e. CIDCO/IRCON.
No claim for interest will be entertained by the corporation in respect of any
balance payments or any deposit which may be held up with the corporation
due to any dispute between the Corporation and sub-contractor or in respect of
any delay on the part of the corporation in making monthly or final payments or
otherwise."
Emphasis supplied.
8. Section 31(7) of the 1996 Act provides for the statutory
mechanism governing the award of interest in arbitral
proceedings, which is reproduced hereunder:

14
"31. Form and contents of arbitral award.-
... (7) (a) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where and in so far as an
arbitral award is for the payment of money, the arbitral tribunal may include in
the sum for which the award is made interest, at such rate as it deems
reasonable, on the whole or any part of the money, for the whole or any part of
the period between the date on which the cause of action arose and the date on
which the award is made.
(b) A sum directed to be paid by an arbitral award shall, unless the award
otherwise directs, carry interest at the rate of two per cent. higher than the
current rate of interest prevalent on the date of award, from the date of award
to the date of payment.
Explanation.-The expression 'current rate of interest' shall have the same
meaning as assigned to it under clause (b) of section 2 of the Interest Act, 1978
(14 of 1978)."
9. Upon perusal of Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act, it is clear
that the power of an Arbitral Tribunal to award interest for
the pre-award period, i.e., from the date on which the cause
of action arose up to the date on which the award is made
(including both pre-reference and pendente lite periods), is
expressly subject to the opening words - "Unless otherwise
agreed by the parties". Section 31(7) of the 1996 Act has to
be construed harmoniously with Section 28(3) of the 1996
Act, which provides for the Arbitral Tribunal to decide in
accordance with the contractual terms governing the parties.
10. The principles governing contractual prohibitions on interest
under Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act have been recently
considered by this Court in Larsen & Toubro Limited
(supra), wherein this Court examined Clause 16(3) read with
Clause 64(5) of the General Conditions of Contract. Clause

15
16(3) expressly prohibited interest on "earnest money and
security deposits or amounts payable to the Contractor under
the Contract", reinforced by Clause 64(5) which provided that
"where the arbitral award is for the payment of money, no
interest shall be payable on whole or any part of the money for
any period till the date on which the award is made".
Reaffirming the law laid down in Sayeed Ahmed (supra),
Sree Kamatchi Amman Constructions v. Divisional
Railway Manager (Works),
8 Bright Power Projects (supra)
and Manraj Enterprises (supra), this Court in Larsen &
Toubro Limited (supra) held that:
"35. On perusal of Section 28(3) and Section 31(7)(a) of the Act, it is clear
that the statutory scheme itself subordinates the discretion of the arbitrator to
the contractual provisions governing interest.
...
43. Now, at this stage, it is pertinent to observe that this Court, thereafter,
in the case of Manraj Enterprises (supra) had an occasion to consider similar
issues involved in the present matter and had considered all the aforementioned
decisions, including the decisions rendered in the cases of Bright Power Projects
(India) (P) Ltd. (supra), Raveechee and Company (supra) and Ambica
Construction vs. Union of India, (2017) 14 SCC 323 (a three-judge bench
judgment of this Court). After considering the aforesaid decisions as well as
several other decisions referred on the issue, this Court has observed in para 8
and 11 as under: ...
"11. In the said decision in Bright Power Projects [Union of India v.
Bright Power Projects (India) (P) Ltd., (2015) 9 SCC 695 : (2015) 4 SCC
(Civ) 702] , this Court also considered Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act. It
is specifically observed and held that Section 31(7) of the 1996 Act, by
using the words "unless otherwise agreed by the parties" categorically
specifies that the arbitrator is bound by the terms of the contract insofar
as award of interest from the date of cause of action to date of the award
is concerned. It is further observed and held that where the parties had
agreed that no interest shall be payable, the Arbitral Tribunal cannot
8
(2010) 8 SCC 767.

16
award interest. Thus, the aforesaid decision of a three-Judge Bench of
this Court is the answer to the submission made on behalf of the
respondent that despite the bar under Clause 16(2) which is applicable
to the parties, the Arbitral Tribunal is not bound by the same. Therefore,
the contention raised on behalf of the respondent that dehors the bar
under Clause 16(2), the Arbitral Tribunal independently and on equitable
ground and/or to do justice can award interest pendente lite or future
interest has no substance and cannot be accepted. Once the contractor
agrees that he shall not be entitled to interest on the amounts payable
under the contract, including the interest upon the earnest money and
the security deposit as mentioned in Clause 16(2) of the
agreement/contract between the parties herein, the arbitrator in the
arbitration proceedings being the creature of the contract has no power
to award interest, contrary to the terms of the agreement/contract
between the parties and contrary to Clause 16(2) of the
agreement/contract in question in this case."
...
45. The provisions of the Act of 1996, including provisions contained in
Section 31(7)(a) give paramount importance to the contract entered into between
the parties and categorically restrict the power of an arbitrator to award pre-award/pendente lite interest when the parties have themselves agreed to the
contrary. Thus, the AT cannot award pre-award/pendente lite interest, even in
the form of compensation, in view of specific Clause 16(3) of GCC read with
Clause 64(5) of GCC."
Emphasis supplied.
11. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that the concluding
phrase "or otherwise" of Clause 26 of the SCC must be
interpreted applying the principles of ejusdem generis and
noscitur a sociis to take colour from the preceding expressions
concerning delay in releasing monthly or final payments and
the expression "or otherwise" is restricted to withholding
interest on delayed interim bills and cannot operate as an
absolute bar against the grant of interest on substantive
claims allowed by the Arbitral Tribunal.
12. However, we are unable to agree with the said contention. The
doctrine of ejusdem generis becomes applicable only where

17
the preceding terms of the general phrase follow a specific
class forming a genus, thereby imparting the specific
character to the subsequent general phrase. At this stage, it
is relevant to note that where the provisions in a contract are
disjunctively joined by the word "or", every such phrase has
to be examined independently due to its wide amplitude. The
same issue was considered in Manraj Enterprises (supra)
and subsequently reiterated in paragraphs 38 and 39 of
Larsen & Toubro Limited (supra):
"38. This Court in the decision rendered in the case of Manraj Enterprises
(supra) has considered a similar submission canvassed on behalf of the party
concerned and thereafter observed and held in para 12.1 as under:
"12.1. It is required to be noted that Clause 16(1) is with respect to
earnest money/security deposit. However, Clause 16(2) is specifically
with respect to interest payable upon the earnest money or the security
deposit or amounts payable to the contractor under the contract. The
words used in Clause 16(2) is "or". Therefore, the expression "amounts
payable to the contractor under the contract" cannot be read in
conjunction with "earnest money deposit" or "security deposit" by
applying the principle of ejusdem generis. The expression "amounts
payable to the contractor under the contract" has to be read
independently and disjunctively to earnest money deposit and security
deposit as the word used is "or" and not "and" between "earnest money
deposit", "security deposit" and "amounts payable to the contractor
under the contract". Therefore, the principle of ejusdem generis is not
applicable in the present case."
39. Thus, it can be said that the rule of ejusdem generis is a tool of
interpretation and is applicable only where the general words follow a specific
class forming a genus. The expression "amounts payable to the contractor under
the contract" used in Clause 16(3) is independent, distinct and of wide
amplitude, and cannot be read down to defeat its plain meaning. Thus, the
submission canvassed by the learned counsel for the respondent cannot be
accepted."
Emphasis supplied.
13. Applying these principles to Clause 26 of the SCC in the
present case, the Clause enumerates the following separate

18
and distinct events disjunctively joined by the conjunction
"or":
(i) any balance payments or any deposits - which may be held
up with the corporation due to any dispute arising between
the Corporation and the sub-contractor, OR
(ii) in respect of any delay on the part of the corporation in
making monthly or final payments, OR
(iii) otherwise.
14. On careful consideration, it can be inferred that the preceding
terms of the phrase "or otherwise" do not constitute a single,
narrow genus restricted to delayed running payments and
also include balance payments, withheld deposits and
amounts withheld due to disputes. Consequently, the
expression "or otherwise" is residuary in nature and has been
consciously incorporated with wide amplitude to encompass
every other conceivable circumstance under which a claim for
interest might be asserted against the Corporation. In
Lilavati Bai v. State of Bombay,
9 the Constitution Bench
of this Court held that the words "or otherwise" cannot be
restricted by reference to the preceding expressions and were
held to be words of extension and not limitation. Thus,
9
(1957) 1 SCC 411.

19
restricting the scope of the expression "or otherwise" to only
delays in monthly or final payments would render the term
redundant and would amount to rewriting the contract
entered into between the parties.
15. The reliance placed by the appellant upon Oil and Natural
Gas Corporation Ltd. (supra) is also misplaced. In the said
decision, the contractual clause was narrowly worded as "no
interest shall be payable by ONGC on any delayed payment /
disputed claim", and did not incorporate any residuary
expression and thus, this Court observed that a stipulation
merely restricting interest on delayed payments cannot be
construed as an absolute bar on pendente lite interest.
However, in the said case, this Court itself recognized that
where the contract prohibits granting pendente lite interest
either expressly or by necessary implication as in the case of
Sayeed Ahmed (supra) and Jaiprakash Associates
Limited (supra), the power of the arbitral tribunal to grant
pendente lite interest stands excluded.
16. In contrast, in the present case, Clause 26 of the SCC
concludes with the residuary phrase "or otherwise". In
Sayeed Ahmed (supra), the clause provided "G1.09. No claim

20
for interest or damages will be entertained by the Government
with respect to any money or balance which may be lying with
the Government or any become due owing to any dispute,
difference or misunderstanding between the Engineer-in-Charge on the one hand and the contractor on the other hand
or with respect to any delay on the part of the Engineer-in-Charge in making periodical or final payment or any other
respect whatsoever." A similar clause was in question in the
decision of Jaiprakash Associates Limited (supra).
Therefore, the High Court rightly concluded that
incorporating the residuary term "or otherwise" stands on
identical footing with the terminology "or any other respect
whatsoever" interpreted in Sayeed Ahmed (supra) and
Jaiprakash Associates Limited (supra), thereby operating
as a contractual prohibition against granting pre-reference as
well as pendente lite interest.
17. At this stage, it is also imperative to observe the distinction
between pre-award interest under Section 31(7)(a) and post-award interest under Section 31(7)(b) of the 1996 Act, i.e.,
Section 31(7)(a) is expressly subject to the contract between
the parties whereas, Section 31(7)(b) provides for grant of

21
post-award interest unless the arbitral tribunal orders
otherwise. This Court in Larsen & Toubro Limited (supra)
observed as under:
"47. With regard to the post-award interest, Section 31(7)(b) of the Act
provides that unless the award otherwise directs, the sum awarded shall carry
interest from the date of the award till payment. The legislative intent underlying
this provision is twofold: first, to compensate the successful party for delayed
realization of the award, and second, to ensure prompt compliance with the
award by the judgment-debtor.
48. Recently, this Court in the case of R.P. Garg (supra), has observed and
held in para 9, 11 and 12 as under:
"... 11. So far as the entitlement of the post-award interest is
concerned, sub-Section (b) of Section 31(7) provides that the sum directed
to be paid by the Arbitral Tribunal shall carry interest. The rate of interest
can be provided by the Arbitrator and in default the statutory
prescription will apply. Clause (b) of Section 31(7) is therefore in contrast
with clause (a) and is not subject to party autonomy. In other words,
clause (b) does not give the parties the right to "contract out" interest for
the post-award period. The expression 'unless the award otherwise
directs' in Section 31(7)(b) relates to rate of interest and not entitlement
of interest. The only distinction made by Section 31(7)(b) is that the rate
of interest granted under the Award is to be given precedence over the
statutorily prescribed rate. The assumption of the High Court that
payment of the interest for the post award period is subject to the
contract is a clear error. ..."
Emphasis supplied.
Therefore, the High Court rightly recognized this statutory
distinction and restricted its interference to setting aside the
pre-reference and pendente lite interest, while maintaining
the award of post-award interest in favour of the appellant.
18. In light of the aforesaid analysis and discussion, the learned
Arbitrator, being a creature of the contract, acted beyond his
jurisdiction in granting pre-reference and pendente lite
interest in contravention of Clause 26 of the SCC, which

22
attracts Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act. Thus, the High Court
rightly acted under Sections 34 and 37 of the 1996 Act in
setting aside the arbitral award dated 28.07.2016 to that
limited extent, while maintaining the substantive claims of
the appellant and post-award interest in favour of the
appellant. Therefore, we find no error in the impugned
judgment dated 20.03.2026 passed by the Division Bench of
the High Court of Delhi in FAO(OS) (COMM) No. 18 of 2026,
affirming the judgment of the learned Single Judge dated
19.11.2025 in O.M.P. (COMM) No. 215 of 2022.
19. Accordingly, the present appeal is dismissed.
20. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.
....................................J.
[ARAVIND KUMAR]
....................................J.
[VIPUL M. PANCHOLI]
NEW DELHI
OCTOBER 15, 2026
